prompts.title: Set up my longbook
phrases: Read my 6-month bank statement and help me set up my longbook
Read my 12-month bank statement and help me set up my longbook
Set up my longbook
aliases: Read my 6-months bank statement along with my onboarding info and help me set up my longbook using longbook's connector and longbook.app/mcp
Read my 12-months bank statement along with my onboarding info and help me set up my longbook using longbook's connector and longbook.app/mcp
Read my bank statement and set up my longbook
prompts.attachments: bank and card statements, ideally the last 6 months, as a PDF with text, an .xlsx or a CSV. Card statements matter too: a bank statement shows only the card bill payment, not what the card was spent on.
prompts.result: Your longbook filled from your statements: every charge on record, the names you picked in setup filled in where your statements or your answers show them, each account's closing balance set, the charges that clearly repeat planned ahead, and the rest set to repeat once you confirm them. It waits in the Proposals screen for you to keep.
procedure: 1. Check that you are allowed to write to the user's longbook. If not, tell the user which setting to switch on, and stop.

2. Read the user's statements in the chat. Through the Mac connection, also read the ones in the longbook documents folder. If there are none, ask the user to attach them, and stop. If only bank statements came, ask for the card statements too.
3. Before reading a line, say which account and which days each statement covers, and today's date.

4. Read what the user's longbook already holds: members, accounts, commitments, charges, categories, the names still waiting to be filled in from setup, and the hints setup kept. Know what longbook can hold for each commitment, charge, member and account before you write. Reports are not among them: longbook draws them itself.

5. Look for the waiting names in the statements first, loosely. A transfer to a person on the 1st of every month could be a salary; a premium line to an insurer could be a health insurance. Record each one under exactly the name the user picked ("Cook salary", not "Ramesh"), so it leaves the waiting list. Keep the waiting names you cannot find for the questions at the end.

6. Use what setup kept. Its hints name the user's accounts by kind ("Savings account") and the people they pay by role ("Maid"): read the statements with them in mind, and add each account or person under the name the statement or the user gives ("HDFC savings 4521", the last four digits at most), never under the hint's word. If an older setup added an account by its kind instead, rename that account to the statement's account first, then record its charges under the new name; recording under a new name first would add a second account. "Self" is the user. A member an older setup added by role is renamed once the user gives the name. Never add a second one.

7. Record every line that is a charge, however small, as paid, on its account. A line that belongs to something already in the longbook is recorded on it, never as a second copy. Name each one the way the user would say it ("Netflix", not the bank's reference).

8. Guess by how much a wrong guess would cost. Copy the amount, the date, the account and the currency exactly as the statement prints them; never guess those. Guess the name, the category, and which commitment a line belongs to, write them, and show them in the table at the end. Ask before writing who a payment is for.

9. Set a charge to repeat when the statement shows the same payee at least three times, a steady month, quarter or year apart, still going at the statement's end: plan it 24 months ahead, set its price to its latest amount if that changed, and show it in the table. Through a sign-in or a key, the rows you wrote reach the longbook only when the user's app is next open, so list these repeats in the table as ones you will set, and set them after the user answers. Record a repeat that stopped before the statement's end as stopped. A charge seen once or twice that may repeat, such as a yearly premium, is not set to repeat: put your guess of how often in the questions.
10. Record money in (salary, a refund, interest, cashback) as money in, kept apart from spending.

11. Write every line, including card bill payments, ATM or cash withdrawals, payments to their own savings and wallet top-ups, as one-time rows like the rest. Only a line between two accounts owned by people tagged self is a transfer, and longbook marks those by itself.

12. Set each account's balance to its statement's closing balance, dated the statement's last day. If a statement prints none, leave the balance alone and say so at the end. Never work one out yourself.

13. Count what you wrote. If a waiting name or a yearly charge, such as a premium, may fall before the statements' first day, or the statements held only a few charges, ask for older or longer statements before guessing anything. Never write anything a second time because the longbook looks unchanged: through a sign-in or a key, your changes reach it only when the user's app is next open.
14. In the end, when responding:

1. Send one table of what is now in the user's longbook, by category: how many charges and the total in each, and the names and categories you guessed. List the repeats you set, with how often and how far ahead they are planned, and every charge you could not place, with its date and amount, at the bottom.

2. Ask, in one message: for each charge seen once or twice that may come round, your guess of how often; what the unplaced charges were; for each waiting name you could not find, one line with your question and your best guess ("Health insurance: which insurer, how much, which month? My guess: the premium line on 15 March"); and anything wrong in the table, a guessed name, category or repeat included. Recommend the user answer by voice.

3. In the same message, explain in one sentence that longbook can remember who a payment is for, and ask whether the user wants to add anyone: a spouse, a child, a parent, or someone they employ, like a cook or a driver. First names are enough. For each person setup named by role, such as "Maid", ask their first name.
15. After the user answers:
1. Apply the corrections and additions in one pass. Undo a repeat the user says is not one.

2. Set each further repeat the user confirms to continue, planned 24 months ahead unless they say otherwise. Through a sign-in or a key, set the repeats you listed too, once the rows are in the longbook; if they are not there yet, ask the user to open longbook first.

3. Tell the user it is done: how many commitments, what repeats and how far ahead it is planned, how many months of reports longbook will draw, the balances set, what was skipped and why, and the two or three things you noticed they may want to change. Say it is waiting in the Proposals screen.

4. Suggest what comes next, leaving out what the user already uses: the other prompts in the Automations section; keeping statements in the longbook documents folder, which their AI can read through the Mac connection; the Siri phrases "Add an expense in my longbook", "Add a commitment in my longbook" and "What's my next commitment in my longbook"; the longbook widget on their iPhone, which shows the next payment; and the longbook Mac app, which shows the next payment in the menu bar.

Through a sign-in or a key, the rows you wrote reach the longbook only when the user's app is next open, so list these repeats in the table as ones you will set, and set them after the user answers. Record a repeat that stopped before the statement's end as stopped. A charge seen once or twice that may repeat, such as a yearly premium, is not set to repeat: put your guess of how often in the questions.

14. In the end, when responding:
1. Send a table of what was added, grouped by category, with the charges under each, the names and categories you guessed, and the repeats you set. Put the ones you could not place at the bottom.

2. Ask, in one message, what the statement could not tell you: what an unknown payee was, who a payment was for, and how often each charge seen once or twice comes round, with your guesses. Ask the user to correct anything you guessed wrong. Recommend the user answer by voice.

1. Apply the answers in one pass. Undo a repeat the user says is not one.

2. List every commitment without a category, past one-off charges included (the app shows them under "No category"), with what each has been charging. The charges are often the clue.
3. Read the user's own category names first, then longbook's built-in categories.

2. Send one table of the categories you guessed: name, date, amount, and the category you chose. Ask the user to correct any that are wrong, and recommend they answer by voice.

1. Apply the corrections in one pass. Keep a category the user names in their own words.
2. Say it is waiting in the Proposals screen.

prompts.title: Add a month report in my longbook
phrases: Add September month report in my longbook
prompts.template: Add {month} month report in my longbook
prompts.attachments: the bank and card statements that cover the month.
prompts.result: The month's statements recorded, the charges they prove confirmed, and each account's balance set. longbook draws that month's report, with "Not yet confirmed" beside the total until every charge in it is confirmed.
procedure: 1. Check that you are allowed to write to the user's longbook. If not, tell the user which setting to switch on, and stop.
2. Say which month you are working on, and today's date.
3. Read the month's charges, and note the passed ones nobody has confirmed: no statement, mail or word from the user behind them. They are what makes the month's report say "Not yet confirmed".
4. Find the month's statements: in the chat first, then, through the Mac connection, in the longbook documents folder. If any are missing, ask the user to attach them.
5. Import each statement as in "Add my statement". A charge nobody had confirmed is confirmed by the statement line that proves it, in place, never as a second copy.
6. Set each account's balance to its statement's closing balance, dated the statement's last day.
7. Never write the report yourself, and never fill a gap with an estimate. longbook draws the report from the charges.
8. In the end, when responding:
1. Say what was added and what was confirmed.
2. Say longbook draws the month's report the next time the app opens, with "Not yet confirmed" beside the total until every passed charge in the month is confirmed.
3. Say it is waiting in the Proposals screen.

prompts.title: Add email invoices in my longbook
phrases: Add email invoices in my longbook
prompts.attachments: none. The user's mail must be connected to their AI.
prompts.result: This month's bank alerts, receipts, bills and money in from your mail, each recorded once, with nothing doubled.
procedure: 1. Check that you are allowed to write to the user's longbook. If not, tell the user which setting to switch on, and stop.
2. Check that you can read the user's mail. If not, say a mail connector is needed, and stop.
3. Search the mail from the 1st of this month to today for money that moved or is due.
4. Read what the longbook already holds: accounts with their last four digits, members, commitments, and charges since the 1st. A mail whose amount and day are already recorded is skipped.

5. From each mail, take only: the amount and its currency; the day the money moved, which is not always the day the mail arrived; who it went to or came from, as a plain name, never a UPI ID or payment address; the account whose last four digits the mail shows; a category; and a member only when the longbook holds them.
6. Record each mail once, by its kind:
1. A bank or card debit alert is a paid charge. When it pays a commitment the longbook holds, it is that commitment's payment, not a new one.

2. An autopay chain (consent, OTP, "deducted", "paid") is one payment, recorded from the mail that says the money left. A pre-debit notice naming a new amount for a commitment is mentioned in the report.
3. A receipt or invoice from a seller is usually the same money as an alert. Record it once and let the receipt give the better name, category and note. A receipt paid in cash is a charge of its own.
4. A bill that is due: when the longbook holds it, check its next charge's date and amount, and add nothing. Otherwise, add an unpaid charge at the due date.
5. Money in, once the bank says it was credited, is money in. A notice that a refund is on its way is not.

6. An insurance or renewal notice: when the longbook holds it, check the next charge against it, and correct it only when the notice comes from the payee itself; otherwise, mention the difference. When the longbook does not hold it, add one unpaid charge at the due date, and propose how often it repeats in the report.

7. A credit card statement is one card bill, named for the card and the month it falls due ("Coral card bill, October 2026"), at the total due, on that card, unpaid, at its due date, recorded as a charge like any other, and a transfer only once both its accounts belong to a person whose Relationship is Self. A bill already recorded for that month is corrected, never added twice.
8. A card bill payment marks that month's card bill paid.

9. Skip wallet top-ups, transfers to the user's own accounts, and investments, unless the longbook holds that payment as a commitment of its own, such as a monthly investment plan: then it is that commitment's payment. Skip OTPs, sign-in alerts, offers, newsletters, brokerage and fund statements, tax notices, and any mail with no amount.
7. Use the last four digits of a card or account only to match. Never write a card or account number, an OTP or a tax ID.
8. In the end, when responding:
1. Say how many charges were added, and which mails were skipped and why, in a line.
2. Say what needs the user's word: something that looks recurring, or an account the longbook does not hold.
3. Say it is waiting in the Proposals screen.

prompts.title: Set up a daily longbook email round
phrases: Go to longbook.app/mcp and set up a daily email round for my longbook, as longbook recommends
aliases: Go to longbook.app/mcp and set yourself up for a daily longbook email round, as longbook recommends
Set yourself up for a daily longbook email round
prompts.attachments: none. The user's mail must be connected, and their AI's app must support scheduled tasks.
prompts.result: Your AI reads your mail every morning at 6 and records the money that moved, so your longbook stays current without you asking.
procedure: 1. Check that you are allowed to write to the user's longbook. If not, tell the user which setting to switch on, and stop.
2. Check that you can read the user's mail. If not, say a mail connector is needed, and stop.

3. Create a scheduled task that runs every day at 6 in the morning, in the user's time zone. Its instruction: read longbook's daily email round method from the longbook connector, then do one round. Each morning then follows the method as it stands that day.
4. If your app has no scheduled tasks, say so, and offer to run the round whenever the user asks.
5. Run the first round now, so the user sees in the Proposals screen what a morning looks like.
6. Each round:
1. First fix anything from an earlier round that the app could not apply, using the real names in the longbook, and file it again in place of the failed one.
2. Read the last day of mail, 36 hours to be safe, and record it as in "Add email invoices in my longbook".
3. Only add, and mark paid what a mail proves. Never cancel, never change a price unless the notice comes from the payee itself, and never decide that something repeats; propose those in the report.
4. When a mail marks a charge paid and nothing is planned after it, plan the next one, one cycle on, at its current price, and say so in the report.
5. End with a short report: what was added, what was skipped, what needs the user's word, and that it is waiting in the Proposals screen. Then stop.
7. In the end, when responding:
1. Say the round is set for 6 every morning, show what the first round added, and say it is waiting in the Proposals screen.

prompts.title: Add document invoices in my longbook
phrases: Add document invoices in my longbook
prompts.attachments: invoices, receipts and bills: attached in the chat, or kept in the longbook documents folder as a PDF with text, an .xlsx or a CSV. A photo or a scanned receipt can be read only when attached in the chat.
prompts.result: The invoices, receipts and bills you attach, or keep in the longbook documents folder, recorded as charges with the file's name in their notes, without doubling what your statements or mail already recorded.
procedure: 1. Check that you are allowed to write to the user's longbook. If not, tell the user which setting to switch on, and stop.

2. Find the files: in the chat first, then, through the Mac connection, in the longbook documents folder. Look in the Mac's own Documents and Downloads folders only if your app can read files there. Otherwise, ask the user to attach them.
3. Treat each invoice or receipt as one charge. It is paid on the day it names when it says paid or that day has passed. It is unpaid at its due date when the due date is ahead.
4. Name it the way the user would say it ("Plumber, kitchen tap"), never by the invoice number. Take the amount, the currency and the day only as printed.

5. Search the longbook first. A charge already recorded from a mail or a statement, for the same amount and day, is the same money: the invoice gives it a better name and note, never a second copy. When the payee is a commitment the longbook holds, the invoice is that commitment's payment.
6. Name the file in the charge's notes. Never copy its contents.
7. In the end, when responding:
1. List what was added or updated.
2. Say it is waiting in the Proposals screen.

Ask, in one message, for what is missing: the name as the user says it, the amount and currency, how often it repeats or whether it is one time, the first or only charge day, which account pays it, and who it is for. 6. Add the three details that matter for its kind, as listed in the Notes chapter of longbook's guide, as far as the user stated them.
7. In the end, when responding:
1. Say what was added, and how far ahead it is planned.
2. Say it is waiting in the Proposals screen.

prompts.title: What did I spend in a month?
phrases: What did I spend in July in my longbook?
What did I spend in July?
prompts.template: What did I spend in {month} in my longbook?
prompts.attachments: none.
prompts.result: What you spent in that month, and what is not yet confirmed. Through the Mac connection this comes from longbook's report; otherwise from your charges, including ones nobody has confirmed yet. Nothing in your longbook changes.
procedure: 1. Through the Mac connection, read the report for the month the user names, and quote its total, its number of charges and its money in. Never recalculate them.
2. If the report says "Not yet confirmed", say the total is what longbook can account for so far, and offer "Add a month report in my longbook" for that month.

3. If the report shows no change against the month before, say longbook would not draw one: the month is not over, one of the two months is short of confirmed charges, or the month before has no confirmed spending in this currency. Never read that as nothing spent, and never work out a change yourself.
4. If there is no report for that month, say why: nothing in it is confirmed yet. Offer "Add a month report in my longbook".

5. Without the Mac connection, read that month's spending from longbook, and say it counts every charge written for the month, including ones nobody has confirmed and, for a month still running, the ones still to come.
6. In the end, when responding:
1. Answer with the figures, and what they leave out.
2. Write nothing.

6. In the end, when responding:

prompts.title: Create a report in my longbook
phrases: Create a report in my longbook
prompts.attachments: none.
prompts.result: A report over the days, accounts, people and categories you choose, on the Reports screen the next time the app is open. It counts confirmed charges only.
procedure: 1. Check that you are allowed to write to the user's longbook. If not, tell the user which setting to switch on, and stop.

2. Ask, in one message: a name for the report; its first and last day (the first is today or earlier, the last may be ahead, and it covers 366 days at most); which accounts and which members (choosing none means everyone); and categories, only if the user wants to narrow by them. 3. Read the real names of the user's accounts, members and categories, and use them exactly as the longbook holds them. Never create anything to fit a report.
4. Ask longbook to draw the report, once. Never state its figures yourself.
5. In the end, when responding:
1. Say it appears on the Reports screen the next time the app is open, counting confirmed charges only, like every report.
2. Say nothing waits in the Proposals screen. To change what the report says, fix the charges behind it, and longbook redraws it.
